mcqs.question: Why do arithmetic instructions typically set condition flags even when the program doesn't explicitly request them?
options: It's a legacy quirk with no modern purpose
Flags are required to store the arithmetic result itself
The very next conditional branch usually reads those flags to decide whether to jump
Only floating-point instructions set flags, not integer ones
mcqs.explanation: Flags are the hidden channel connecting a comparison/arithmetic op to the branch that follows it — this is how compiled if/while conditions actually work. It's a functioning, load-bearing mechanism (not a legacy leftover), the result itself is stored separately in a register, and both integer and floating-point operations can set relevant flags.

mcqs.question: What fundamentally distinguishes a 'call' instruction from a plain 'jump'?
options: There is no real difference; they're interchangeable
A call can only target memory addresses, while jump can target registers
A call executes faster than a jump on all CPUs
A call also saves a return address so execution can resume afterward
mcqs.explanation: The return address save is what makes function calls possible — the CPU has no innate concept of functions, just jumps with a remembered comeback point. Both call and jump can target registers or memory depending on the ISA, relative speed isn't a defining property, and they are not interchangeable.

mcqs.question: In `cmp x, y` followed by `bgt label`, what does the `cmp` instruction actually do?
options: It computes x minus y, discards the numeric result, and sets condition flags from it
It directly jumps to label if x is greater than y
It stores the result of x minus y into a register for later use
It has no effect unless followed by a store instruction
mcqs.explanation: cmp performs the subtraction purely to derive flags (zero, negative, overflow); the arithmetic result itself is thrown away. The jump decision belongs to the following branch instruction, not cmp itself, no register write occurs, and cmp is meaningful and complete on its own regardless of what follows.

mcqs.question: When would a compiler prefer a conditional-move instruction over a conditional branch for code like `x = a > b ? a : b`?
options: Always — conditional moves are strictly better in every situation
When both branch paths are cheap to compute, so avoiding a possible misprediction outweighs computing the unused side
Only when the target ISA has no branch instructions at all
Never — conditional moves are purely a theoretical construct not used in practice
mcqs.explanation: Conditional-move trades guaranteed extra work (computing both sides) for eliminating misprediction risk — a good trade only when both sides are trivial. It's not universally better (long/expensive branch bodies favor real branches), it isn't reserved for branch-less ISAs, and it's a widely used real compiler optimization.
